title: Chapter 42. Of Ecclesiastical Power
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth
paragraphs: For the understanding of POWER ECCLESIASTICAL — what it is, and in whom — we are to distinguish the time from the ascension of our Saviour into two parts: one before the conversion of kings, and of men endowed with sovereign civil power; the other after their conversion. For it was long after the ascension before any king, or civil sovereign, embraced and publicly allowed the teaching of the Christian religion.

And for the time between, it is plain that ecclesiastical power was in the apostles; and after them, in such as were ordained by them to preach the gospel, and to convert men to Christianity, and to direct those who were converted in the way of salvation. And after these, the power was delivered again to others by those whom they ordained — and this was done by the imposition of hands on those who were ordained, by which was signified the giving of the Holy Spirit, or Spirit of God, to those whom they ordained ministers of God, to advance his kingdom. So that the imposition of hands was nothing but the seal of their commission to preach Christ, and teach his doctrine; and the giving of the Holy Ghost by that ceremony was an imitation of what Moses did. For Moses used the same ceremony with his minister Joshua, as we read in Deuteronomy 34:9: 'And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him.' Our Saviour therefore, between his resurrection and ascension, gave his Spirit to the apostles: first by 'breathing on them and saying' (John 20:22), 'Receive the Holy Spirit'; and after his ascension (Acts 2:2–3) by sending down on them 'a mighty wind, and cloven tongues of fire' — and not by imposition of hands; just as God did not lay his hands on Moses. And his apostles afterward transmitted the same Spirit by the imposition of hands, as Moses did to Joshua. So it is plain by this in whom the ecclesiastical power continually remained, in those first times when there was no Christian commonwealth: namely, in those who received it from the apostles, by successive laying on of hands.

Here we have the person of God borne now the third time. For as Moses, and the high priests, were God's representative in the Old Testament, and our Saviour himself as man during his sojourn on earth, so the Holy Ghost — that is, the apostles and their successors in the office of preaching and teaching, who had received the Holy Spirit — have represented him ever since. But a person (as I have shown before, chapter 16) is one who is represented, as often as he is represented. And so God, who has been represented (that is, personated) thrice, may properly enough be said to be three persons — though neither the word person, nor Trinity, is ascribed to him in the Bible. St John indeed (1 Epist. 5:7) says: 'There are three that bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.' But this does not disagree, but fits well with, three persons in the proper meaning of 'persons' — which is, that which is represented by another. For so God the Father, as represented by Moses, is one person; and as represented by his Son, another person; and as represented by the apostles and the doctors who taught by authority derived from them, is a third person. And yet every person here is the person of one and the same God. But a man may ask, what was it whereof these three bore witness? St John therefore tells us (verse 11) that they bear witness 'that God has given us eternal life in his Son.' Again, if it should be asked, in what does that testimony appear? — the answer is easy. For he has testified the same by the miracles he wrought: first by Moses; secondly, by his Son himself; and lastly, by his apostles, who had received the Holy Spirit. All of these in their times represented the person of God, and either prophesied or preached Jesus Christ. And as for the apostles, it was the character of the apostleship, in the twelve first and great apostles, to bear witness of his resurrection — as appears expressly (Acts 1:21–22), where St Peter, when a new apostle was to be chosen in the place of Judas Iscariot, uses these words: 'Of these men who have accompanied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning at the baptism of John, to that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.' Which words interpret the 'bearing of witness' mentioned by St John. There is in the same place mentioned another trinity of witnesses on earth. For (verse 8) he says, 'There are three that bear witness on earth, the Spirit, and the Water, and the Blood; and these three agree in one' — that is, the graces of God's Spirit, and the two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, which all agree in one testimony, to assure the consciences of believers of eternal life. Of which testimony he says (verse 10), 'He that believes on the Son of man has the witness in himself.' In this trinity on earth, the unity is not of the thing; for the Spirit, the Water, and the Blood are not the same substance, though they give the same testimony. But in the trinity of heaven, the persons are the persons of one and the same God, though represented at three different times and occasions. To conclude, the doctrine of the Trinity, as far as can be gathered directly from Scripture, is in substance this: that God, who is always one and the same, was the person represented by Moses; the person represented by his Son incarnate; and the person represented by the apostles. As represented by the apostles, the Holy Spirit by which they spoke, is God. As represented by his Son (who was God and man), the Son is that God. As represented by Moses and the high priests, the Father — that is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ — is that God. From which we may gather the reason why those names, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in the signification of the Godhead, are never used in the Old Testament: for they are persons — that is, they have their names from representing; which could not be, until different men had represented God's person in ruling, or in directing under him.

Thus we see how the ecclesiastical power was left by our Saviour to the apostles, and how they were (to the end that they might the better exercise that power) endowed with the Holy Spirit, which is therefore called sometimes in the New Testament Paracletus, which signifies an Assister, or one called for help, though it is commonly translated 'Comforter.' Let us now consider the power itself: what it was, and over whom.

Cardinal Bellarmine, in his third General Controversy, has handled a great many questions concerning the ecclesiastical power of the pope of Rome; and he begins with this: whether it ought to be monarchical, aristocratic, or democratic. All these sorts of power are sovereign and coercive. If now it should appear that there is no coercive power left by our Saviour, but only a power to proclaim the kingdom of Christ, and to persuade men to submit to it; and by precepts and good counsel, to teach those who have submitted what they are to do, that they may be received into the kingdom of God when it comes; and that the apostles, and other ministers of the gospel, are our schoolmasters, and not our commanders, and their precepts not laws, but wholesome counsels — then all that dispute is in vain.

I have shown already (in the last chapter) that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world; therefore neither can his ministers (unless they are kings) require obedience in his name. For if the supreme king does not have his regal power in this world, by what authority can obedience be required to his officers? 'As my Father sent me' (so says our Saviour) 'I send you.' But our Saviour was sent to persuade the Jews to return to, and to invite the Gentiles to receive, the kingdom of his Father — not to reign in majesty, not even as his Father's lieutenant, until the day of judgement.

The time between the ascension and the general resurrection is called, not a reigning, but a regeneration — that is, a preparation of men for the second and glorious coming of Christ at the day of judgement. As appears by the words of our Saviour (Matt. 19:28): 'You that have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, you shall also sit on twelve thrones.' And of St Paul (Eph. 6:15): 'Having your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.'

And it is compared by our Saviour to fishing — that is, to winning men to obedience, not by coercion and punishing, but by persuasion. So he did not say to his apostles that he would make them so many Nimrods, hunters of men, but fishers of men. It is compared also to leaven, to the sowing of seed, and to the multiplication of a grain of mustard seed — by all of which compulsion is excluded; and consequently, in that time, there can be no actual reigning. The work of Christ's ministers is evangelisation — that is, a proclamation of Christ, and a preparation for his second coming; as the evangelisation of John the Baptist was a preparation for his first coming.

Again, the office of Christ's ministers in this world is to make men believe, and have faith in, Christ. But faith has no relation to, nor any dependence on, compulsion or commandment, but only on certainty, or probability, of arguments drawn from reason, or from something men already believe. So the ministers of Christ in this world have, by that title, no power to punish any man for not believing, or for contradicting what they say. They have, I say, no power by that title of Christ's ministers, to punish such men. But if they have sovereign civil power by political institution, then indeed they may lawfully punish any contradiction to their laws whatsoever. And St Paul, of himself and other preachers then of the gospel, says in express words (2 Cor. 1:24), 'We have no dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy.'

Another argument that the ministers of Christ in this present world have no right of commanding may be drawn from the lawful authority which Christ has left to all princes, Christian as well as infidel. St Paul says (Col. 3:20), 'Children, obey your parents in all things; for this is well pleasing to the Lord.' And verse 22: 'Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh, not with eye-service as men-pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing the Lord.' This is spoken to those whose masters were infidels; and yet they are bidden to obey them in all things. And again, concerning obedience to princes (Rom. 13, the first six verses): exhorting men to 'be subject to the higher powers,' he says, 'that all power is ordained of God,' and 'that we ought to be subject to them, not only for' fear of incurring their 'wrath, but also for conscience' sake.' And St Peter (1 Epistle 2:13–15): 'Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake — whether to the king as supreme, or to governors, as to those that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of those that do well; for so is the will of God.' And again, St Paul (Tit. 3:1): 'Put men in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, and to obey magistrates.' These princes and powers, of whom St Peter and St Paul here speak, were all infidels; much more, then, are we to obey those Christians whom God has ordained to have sovereign power over us. How then can we be obliged to do anything contrary to the command of the king, or of any other sovereign representative of the commonwealth of which we are members, and by whom we look to be protected? It is therefore plain that Christ has not left to his ministers in this world — unless they are also endowed with civil authority — any authority to command other men.

But what (some may object) if a king, or a senate, or some other sovereign person forbid us to believe in Christ? To this I answer, that such forbidding is of no effect, because belief and unbelief never follow men's commands. Faith is a gift of God, which man can neither give nor take away by promise of rewards, or by menaces of torture. And if it is further asked, what if we are commanded by our lawful prince to say with our tongue that we do not believe — must we obey such a command? Profession with the tongue is only an external thing, and no more than any other gesture by which we signify our obedience; and in this a Christian, holding firmly in his heart the faith of Christ, has the same liberty that the prophet Elisha allowed to Naaman the Syrian. Naaman was converted in his heart to the God of Israel; for he says (2 Kings 5:17): 'Your servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering, nor sacrifice, to other gods but to the Lord. In this thing the Lord pardon your servant: that when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon — when I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, the Lord pardon your servant in this thing.' This the prophet approved, and bade him 'Go in peace.' Here Naaman believed in his heart; but by bowing before the idol Rimmon, he denied the true God in effect, as much as if he had done it with his lips. But then, what shall we answer to our Saviour's saying, 'Whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before my Father which is in heaven'? This we may say: that whatever a subject (as Naaman was) is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, and does not in order to satisfy his own mind, but in order to satisfy the laws of his country, that action is not his, but his sovereign's. Nor is it he that in this case denies Christ before men, but his governor and the law of his country. If any man shall accuse this doctrine as repugnant to true and unfeigned Christianity, I ask him: in case there should be a subject in any Christian commonwealth who in his heart is inwardly of the Mahometan religion, then if his sovereign commands him to be present at the divine service of the Christian church, on pain of death, whether he thinks that Mahometan obliged in conscience to suffer death for that cause, rather than obey that command of his lawful prince? If he says he ought rather to suffer death, then he authorises all private men to disobey their princes in maintenance of their religion, true or false. If he says he ought to be obedient, then he allows to himself what he denies to another — contrary to the words of our Saviour, 'Whatever you would that men should do to you, that do to them'; and contrary to the law of nature (which is the indubitable everlasting law of God), 'Do not to another what you would not he should do to you.'

But what then shall we say of all those martyrs we read of in the history of the church — that they have needlessly cast away their lives? For answer to this, we are to distinguish the persons who have been put to death for that cause. Of these, some have received a calling to preach, and profess, the kingdom of Christ openly; others have had no such calling, nor was more required of them than their own faith. The former sort, if they have been put to death for bearing witness to this point — that Jesus Christ is risen from the dead — were true martyrs. For a martyr is (to give the true definition of the word) a witness of the resurrection of Jesus the Messiah; which none can be but those who conversed with him on earth, and saw him after he was risen. For a witness must have seen what he testifies, or else his testimony is not good. And that none but such can properly be called martyrs of Christ is plain from the words of St Peter, Acts 1:21–22: 'Wherefore, of these men who have accompanied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John to that same day he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a martyr (that is, a witness) with us of his resurrection.' Where we may observe that he who is to be a witness of the truth of the resurrection of Christ — that is, of the truth of this fundamental article of the Christian religion, that Jesus was the Christ — must be some disciple who conversed with him, and saw him before and after his resurrection; and consequently must be one of his original disciples. Whereas they who were not so can witness no more than that their predecessors said it, and so are only witnesses of other men's testimony, and are only second martyrs, or martyrs of Christ's witnesses.

He, that to maintain every doctrine he himself draws out of the history of our Saviour's life, and of the Acts, or Epistles of the apostles, or which he believes on the authority of a private man, will oppose the laws and authority of the civil state, is very far from being a martyr of Christ, or a martyr of his martyrs. It is one article only that, to die for, deserves so honourable a name; and that article is this: that Jesus is the Christ — that is, he who has redeemed us, and shall come again to give us salvation, and eternal life in his glorious kingdom. To die for every tenet that serves the ambition or profit of the clergy is not required; nor is it the death of the witness, but the testimony itself, that makes the martyr. For the word signifies nothing but the man who bears witness, whether he is put to death for his testimony or not.

Also, he who is not sent to preach this fundamental article, but takes it upon himself by his private authority — though he is a witness, and so a martyr, either primary of Christ, or secondary of his apostles, disciples, or their successors — is yet not obliged to suffer death for that cause; because, being not called to it, it is not required at his hands. Nor ought he to complain, if he loses the reward he expects from those who never set him on the work. None therefore can be a martyr, neither of the first nor of the second degree, who has not a warrant to preach Christ come in the flesh — that is, none but such as are sent to the conversion of infidels. For no man is a witness to him who already believes, and therefore needs no witness; but to those who deny, or doubt, or have not heard it. Christ sent his apostles, and his seventy disciples, with authority to preach; he did not send all who believed. And he sent them to unbelievers: 'I send you,' he says, 'as sheep among wolves'; not as sheep among other sheep.
Lastly, the points of their commission, as they are expressly set down in the gospel, contain none of them any authority over the congregation.

We have first (Matt. 10) that the twelve apostles were sent 'to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' and commanded to preach, 'that the kingdom of God was at hand.' Now 'preaching,' in the original, is the act which a crier, herald, or other officer uses to do publicly in proclaiming a king. But a crier has no right to command any man. And (Luke 10:2) the seventy disciples are sent out 'as labourers, not as lords of the harvest,' and are bidden (verse 9) to say, 'The kingdom of God is come near to you.' And by 'kingdom' here is meant, not the kingdom of grace, but the kingdom of glory; for they are bidden to denounce it (verse 11) to those cities which shall not receive them, as a threat: that it shall be more tolerable in that day for Sodom, than for such a city. And (Matt. 20:28) our Saviour tells his disciples, who sought priority of place, that their office was to minister, even as the Son of man came, not to be ministered to, but to minister. Preachers therefore have not magisterial, but ministerial, power. 'Be not called Masters,' says our Saviour (Matt. 23:10), 'for one is your Master, even Christ.'

Another point of their commission is to teach all nations, as it is in Matt. 28:19; or as in St Mark 16:15, 'Go into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.' Teaching therefore and preaching are the same thing. For those who proclaim the coming of a king must withal make known by what right he comes, if they mean men to submit themselves to him — as St Paul did to the Jews of Thessalonica, when 'three Sabbath days he reasoned with them out of the Scriptures, opening and alleging that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead, and that this Jesus is Christ.' But to teach out of the Old Testament that Jesus was the Christ (that is, king) and risen from the dead, is not to say that men are bound, after they believe it, to obey those who tell them so against the laws and commands of their sovereigns; but that they shall do wisely to expect the coming of Christ hereafter, in patience and faith, with obedience to their present magistrates.

Another point of their commission is to baptise, 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.' What is baptism? Dipping into water. But what is it to dip a man into the water in the name of anything? The meaning of these words of baptism is this: he that is baptised is dipped, or washed, as a sign of becoming a new man, and a loyal subject to that God, whose person was represented in old time by Moses and the high priests, when he reigned over the Jews; and to Jesus Christ, his Son, God and man, who has redeemed us, and shall in his human nature represent his Father's person in his eternal kingdom after the resurrection; and to acknowledge that the doctrine of the apostles — who, assisted by the Spirit of the Father, and of the Son, were left for guides to bring us into that kingdom — is the only and assured way to it. This being our promise in baptism, and the authority of earthly sovereigns being not to be put down until the day of judgement (for that is expressly affirmed by St Paul, 1 Cor. 15:22–24, where he says: 'As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive. But every man in his own order: Christ the first fruits; afterward, they that are Christ's, at his coming. Then comes the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom of God, even the Father, when he shall have put down all rule, and all authority, and power'), it is plain that we do not in baptism constitute over us another authority, by which our external actions are to be governed in this life; but promise to take the doctrine of the apostles for our direction in the way to life eternal.

The power of remission and retention of sins — also called the power of loosing and binding, and sometimes the keys of the kingdom of heaven — is a consequence of the authority to baptise, or refuse to baptise. For baptism is the sacrament of allegiance, of those who are to be received into the kingdom of God — that is, into eternal life, that is, to remission of sin. For as eternal life was lost by the committing, so it is recovered by the remitting, of men's sins. The end of baptism is the remission of sins; and therefore St Peter, when those who were converted by his sermon on the day of Pentecost asked what they were to do, advised them to 'repent, and be baptised in the name of Jesus, for the remission of sins.' And so, since to baptise is to declare the reception of men into God's kingdom, and to refuse to baptise is to declare their exclusion, it follows that the power to declare them cast out, or retained in it, was given to the same apostles, and their substitutes, and successors. And so after our Saviour had breathed on them, saying (John 20:22), 'Receive the Holy Ghost,' he adds in the next verse, 'Whose soever sins you remit, they are remitted to them; and whose soever sins you retain, they are retained.' By these words is not granted an authority to forgive, or to retain, sins simply and absolutely, as God forgives or retains them, who knows the heart of man and the truth of his penitence and conversion — but conditionally, to the penitent. And this forgiveness, or absolution, in case the absolved has only a feigned repentance, is thereby — without any other act, or sentence, of the absolver — made void, and has no effect at all to salvation; but on the contrary, to the aggravation of his sin. So the apostles, and their successors, are to follow only the outward marks of repentance; which appearing, they have no authority to deny absolution; and if they do not appear, they have no authority to absolve. The same also is to be observed in baptism. For to a converted Jew, or Gentile, the apostles had not the power to deny baptism; nor to grant it to the unrepentant. But since no man is able to discern the truth of another man's repentance further than by external marks, taken from his words and actions, which are subject to hypocrisy, another question arises: who is constituted judge of those marks? And this question is decided by our Saviour himself (Matt. 18:15–17): 'If your brother (says he) shall trespass against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone; if he shall hear you, you have gained your brother. But if he will not hear you, then take with you one, or two, more. And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it to the church; let him be to you as a heathen man and a publican.' By which it is plain that the judgement concerning the truth of repentance belonged not to any one man, but to the church — that is, to the assembly of the faithful, or to those who have authority to be their representant. But besides the judgement, the pronouncing of sentence is also necessary; and this belonged always to the apostle, or to some pastor of the church, as prolocutor. And of this our Saviour speaks in the 18th verse: 'Whatsoever you shall bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven; and whatsoever you shall loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven.' And in keeping with this was the practice of St Paul (1 Cor. 5:3–5), where he says: 'For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have determined already, as though I were present, concerning him that has so done this deed; in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one to Satan' — that is, to cast him out of the church, as a man whose sins are not forgiven. Paul here pronounces the sentence; but the assembly was first to hear the case (for St Paul was absent), and consequently to condemn him. But in the same chapter (verses 11–12) the judgement in such a case is more expressly attributed to the assembly: 'But now I have written to you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, etc.; with such a one, not even to eat. For what have I to do to judge those that are without? Do not you judge those that are within?' The sentence therefore by which a man was put out of the church was pronounced by the apostle, or pastor; but the judgement concerning the merit of the case was in the church — that is (as the times were, before the conversion of kings, and of men that had sovereign authority in the commonwealth) the assembly of the Christians dwelling in the same city; as in Corinth, in the assembly of the Christians of Corinth.

This part of the power of the keys, by which men were thrust out of the kingdom of God, is what is called excommunication; and to excommunicate, in the original, is aposynagogon poiein, 'to cast out of the synagogue' — that is, out of the place of divine service: a word drawn from the custom of the Jews, to cast out of their synagogues such as they thought, in manners or doctrine, contagious — as lepers were, by the law of Moses, separated from the congregation of Israel, until such time as they should be pronounced clean by the priest.
The use of excommunication without civil power.

The use and effect of excommunication, while it was not yet strengthened with the civil power, was no more than that those who were not excommunicate were to avoid the company of those who were. It was not enough to regard them as heathen who had never been Christians, for with such they might eat and drink — which with excommunicate persons they might not — as appears by the words of St Paul (1 Cor. 5:9 etc.), where he tells them he had formerly forbidden them to 'company with fornicators'; but (because that could not be done without going out of the world) he restrained it to such fornicators, and otherwise vicious persons, as were of the brethren: 'with such a one,' he says, they ought not to keep company, 'no, not to eat.' And this is no more than what our Saviour says (Matt. 18:17), 'Let him be to you as a heathen, and as a publican.' For publicans (which signifies tax-farmers, and receivers of the revenue of the commonwealth) were so hated and detested by the Jews who had to pay it that 'publican' and 'sinner' were taken among them for the same thing — so much so that when our Saviour accepted the invitation of Zacchaeus, a publican, although it was to convert him, it was raised against him as a crime. And so, when our Saviour added 'publican' to 'heathen,' he did forbid them to eat with a man excommunicate.

As for keeping them out of their synagogues, or places of assembly, they had no power to do it but that of the owner of the place, whether he were Christian or heathen. And because all places are by right in the dominion of the commonwealth, as well he who was excommunicated, as he who had never been baptised, might enter into them by commission from the civil magistrate — as Paul before his conversion entered into the synagogues at Damascus (Acts 9:2) to apprehend Christians, men and women, and to carry them bound to Jerusalem, by commission from the high priest.

By which it appears that upon a Christian who should become an apostate, in a place where the civil power did persecute, or did not assist, the church, the effect of excommunication had nothing in it, neither of damage in this world, nor of terror. Not of terror, because of their unbelief; nor of damage, because they returned thereby into the favour of the world; and in the world to come, were to be in no worse estate than those who never had believed. The damage redounded rather to the church, by the provocation of those they cast out, to a freer exercise of their malice.

Excommunication therefore had its effect only on those who believed that Jesus Christ was to come again in glory, to reign over and to judge both the quick and the dead, and would therefore refuse entrance into his kingdom to those whose sins were retained — that is, to those who were excommunicated by the church. And thence it is that St Paul calls excommunication a delivering of the excommunicate person to Satan. For outside the kingdom of Christ, all other kingdoms after the judgement are comprehended in the kingdom of Satan. This is what the faithful stood in fear of, so long as they stood excommunicate — that is, in a state in which their sins were not forgiven. From which we may understand that excommunication, in the time when the Christian religion was not authorised by the civil power, was used only for the correction of manners, not of errors in opinion. For it is a punishment of which none could be sensible but such as believed, and expected the coming again of our Saviour to judge the world; and those who so believed needed no other opinion, but only uprightness of life, to be saved.

Excommunication lies for injustice: as (Matt. 18) 'If your brother offend you, tell it him privately; then with witnesses; lastly, tell the church; and then if he does not obey, let him be to you as a heathen man, and a publican.' And excommunication lies for a scandalous life, as (1 Cor. 5:11): 'If any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or an extortioner, with such a one you are not to eat.' But to excommunicate a man who held this foundation — that Jesus was the Christ — for difference of opinion in other points, by which that foundation was not destroyed, there appears no authority in Scripture, nor example in the apostles. There is indeed in St Paul (Titus 3:10) a text that seems to be to the contrary: 'A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, reject.' For a heretic is one who, being a member of the church, nevertheless teaches some private opinion which the church has forbidden; and such a one, St Paul advises Titus, after the first and second admonition, to reject. But to 'reject' (in this place) is not to excommunicate the man, but to give over admonishing him, to let him alone, to set by disputing with him, as one who is to be convinced only by himself. The same apostle says (2 Tim. 2:23), 'Foolish and unlearned questions avoid.' The word 'avoid' in this place, and 'reject' in the former, is the same in the original: paraitou. But foolish questions may be set by, without excommunication. And again (Tit. 3:9), 'Avoid foolish questions,' where the original, periistaso ('set them by'), is equivalent to the former word 'reject.' There is no other place that can so much as colourably be drawn to countenance the casting out of the church faithful men — such as believed the foundation, only for a singular superstructure of their own, proceeding perhaps from a good and pious conscience. But on the contrary, all such passages as command avoiding such disputes are written for a lesson to pastors (such as Timothy and Titus were) not to make new articles of faith, by determining every small controversy, which obliges men to a needless burden of conscience, or provokes them to break the union of the church. Which lesson the apostles themselves observed well. St Peter and St Paul, though their controversy was great (as we may read in Gal. 2:11), yet they did not cast one another out of the church. Nevertheless, during the apostles' time, there were other pastors who did not observe it: as Diotrephes (3 John 9 etc.), who cast out of the church such as St John himself thought fit to be received into it, out of a pride he took in pre-eminence; so early it was, that vainglory and ambition had found entrance into the church of Christ.

For a man to be liable to excommunication, there are many conditions requisite. First, that he be a member of some community — that is, of some lawful assembly, that is, of some Christian church that has power to judge of the cause for which he is to be excommunicated. For where there is no community, there can be no excommunication; nor where there is no power to judge, can there be any power to give sentence. From this it follows that one church cannot be excommunicated by another. For either they have equal power to excommunicate each other — in which case excommunication is not discipline, nor an act of authority, but schism, and dissolution of charity; or one is so subordinate to the other that they both have but one voice, and then they are but one church, and the part excommunicated is no longer a church, but a dissolute number of individual persons.

And because the sentence of excommunication implies an advice not to keep company, nor so much as to eat, with him who is excommunicate, if a sovereign prince, or assembly, be excommunicate, the sentence is of no effect. For all subjects are bound to be in the company and presence of their own sovereign (when he requires it) by the law of nature; nor can they lawfully either expel him from any place of his own dominion, whether profane or holy, nor go out of his dominion without his leave; much less (if he calls them to that honour) refuse to eat with him. And as to other princes and states, because they are not parts of one and the same congregation, they need not any other sentence to keep them from keeping company with the state excommunicate. For the very institution, as it unites many men into one community, so it dissociates one community from another; so that excommunication is not needed for keeping kings and states asunder, nor has any further effect than is in the nature of policy itself — unless it be to instigate princes to war upon one another.

Nor is the excommunication of a Christian subject, who obeys the laws of his own sovereign (whether Christian or heathen), of any effect. For if he believes that 'Jesus is the Christ, he has the Spirit of God' (1 John 4:1), 'and God dwells in him, and he in God' (1 John 4:15). But he who has the Spirit of God; he who dwells in God; he in whom God dwells, can receive no harm by the excommunication of men. So he who believes Jesus to be the Christ is free from all the dangers threatened to persons excommunicate. He who does not believe it, is no Christian. So a true and unfeigned Christian is not liable to excommunication; nor is even a professed Christian, until his hypocrisy appears in his manners — that is, until his behaviour is contrary to the law of his sovereign, which is the rule of manners, and which Christ and his apostles have commanded us to be subject to. For the church cannot judge of manners but by external actions; and those actions can never be unlawful, except when they are against the law of the commonwealth.

If a man's father, mother, or master is excommunicate, the children are still not forbidden to keep them company, nor to eat with them; for that would be (for the most part) to oblige them not to eat at all, for want of means to get food, and to authorise them to disobey their parents, and masters, contrary to the precept of the apostles.

In short, the power of excommunication cannot be extended further than the end for which the apostles and pastors of the church have their commission from our Saviour — which is not to rule by command and coaction, but by teaching and directing men in the way of salvation in the world to come. And as a master in any science may abandon his scholar, when he stubbornly neglects the practice of his rules, but cannot accuse him of injustice, because he was never bound to obey him, so a teacher of Christian doctrine may abandon his disciples that obstinately continue in an unchristian life; but he cannot say they do him wrong, because they are not obliged to obey him. For to a teacher who shall so complain may be applied the answer of God to Samuel in the like case (1 Sam. 8): 'They have not rejected you, but me.' Excommunication therefore, when it lacks the assistance of the civil power (as it does when a Christian state or prince is excommunicated by a foreign authority), is without effect, and consequently ought to be without terror. The name fulmen excommunicationis (that is, the thunderbolt of excommunication) proceeded from an imagining of the bishop of Rome — who first used it — that he was king of kings, as the heathens made Jupiter king of the gods, and assigned him, in their poems and pictures, a thunderbolt, with which to subdue and punish the giants that should dare to deny his power. Which imagining was grounded on two errors: one, that the kingdom of Christ is of this world, contrary to our Saviour's own words, 'My kingdom is not of this world'; the other, that he is Christ's vicar, not only over his own subjects, but over all the Christians of the world — for which there is no ground in Scripture, and the contrary shall be proved in its due place.

St Paul, coming to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews (Acts 17:2–3), 'as his manner was, went in to them; and three Sabbath days reasoned with them out of the Scriptures, opening, and alleging, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead; and that this Jesus whom he preached was the Christ.' The Scriptures here mentioned were the Scriptures of the Jews — that is, the Old Testament. The men, to whom he was to prove that Jesus was the Christ, and risen again from the dead, were also Jews, and already believed that they were the word of God. Hereupon (as it is in verse 4) some of them believed; and (as it is in verse 5) some believed not. What was the reason, when they all believed the Scripture, that they did not all believe alike — but some approved, others disapproved, the interpretation of St Paul who cited them, and every one interpreted them for himself? It was this: St Paul came to them without any legal commission, and in the manner of one who would not command, but persuade. Which he had to do, either by miracles, as Moses did to the Israelites in Egypt, that they might see his authority in God's works; or by reasoning from the already received Scripture, that they might see the truth of his doctrine in God's word. But whoever persuades by reasoning from principles written makes him to whom he speaks judge both of the meaning of those principles and of the force of his inferences upon them. If these Jews of Thessalonica were not, who else was the judge of what St Paul alleged out of Scripture? If St Paul, what need had he to quote any passages to prove his doctrine? It would have been enough to say, 'I find it so in Scripture' — that is, in your laws, of which I am interpreter, as sent by Christ. The interpreter therefore of the Scripture, to whose interpretation the Jews of Thessalonica were bound to stand, could be none; every one might believe, or not believe, according as the allegations seemed to himself to be agreeable, or not agreeable, to the meaning of the places alleged. And generally, in all cases of the world, he who claims any proof makes judge of his proof him to whom he addresses his speech. And as to the case of the Jews in particular, they were bound by express words (Deut. 17) to receive the determination of all hard questions from the priests and judges of Israel for the time being. But this is to be understood of the Jews who were yet unconverted.

For the conversion of the Gentiles, there was no use in alleging the Scriptures, which they did not believe. The apostles therefore laboured by reason to refute their idolatry; and, that done, to persuade them to the faith of Christ, by their testimony of his life and resurrection. So that there could not yet be any controversy concerning the authority to interpret Scripture, seeing no man was obliged, during his infidelity, to follow any man's interpretation of any Scripture, except his sovereign's interpretation of the laws of his country.

Let us now consider the conversion itself, and see what there was in it that could be the cause of such an obligation. Men were converted to no other thing than the belief of what the apostles preached. And the apostles preached nothing but that Jesus was the Christ — that is, the king who was to save them, and reign over them eternally in the world to come; and consequently that he was not dead, but risen again from the dead, and gone up into heaven, and should come again one day to judge the world (which also should rise again to be judged), and reward every man according to his works. None of them preached that himself, or any other apostle, was such an interpreter of the Scripture that all who became Christians ought to take their interpretation for law. For to interpret the laws is part of the administration of a present kingdom, which the apostles had not. They prayed then, and all other pastors ever since, 'Your kingdom come,' and exhorted their converts to obey their then-Ethnic princes. The New Testament was not yet published in one body. Every one of the evangelists was interpreter of his own gospel; and every apostle of his own epistle. And of the Old Testament, our Saviour himself says to the Jews (John 5:39), 'Search the Scriptures; for in them you think to have eternal life, and they are they that testify of me.' If he had not meant they should interpret them, he would not have bidden them take from them the proof of his being the Christ; he would have interpreted them himself, or referred them to the interpretation of the priests.

When a difficulty arose, the apostles and elders of the church assembled themselves together, and determined what should be preached, and taught, and how they should interpret the Scriptures to the people; but they did not take from the people the liberty to read, and interpret, them to themselves. The apostles sent various letters to the churches, and other writings for their instruction; which would have been in vain, if they had not allowed them to interpret — that is, to consider the meaning of them. And as it was in the apostles' time, it must be until such time as there should be pastors who could authorise an interpreter, whose interpretation should generally be stood to. But that could not be until kings were pastors, or pastors kings.

There are two senses in which a writing may be said to be canonical. For 'canon' signifies a rule; and a rule is a precept by which a man is guided, and directed, in any action whatever. Such precepts, though given by a teacher to his disciple, or a counsellor to his friend, without power to compel him to observe them, are nevertheless canons, because they are rules. But when they are given by one whom he who receives them is bound to obey, then those canons are not only rules, but laws. The question therefore here is of the power to make the Scriptures (which are the rules of Christian faith) laws.

That part of the Scripture which was first law was the Ten Commandments, written on two tables of stone, and delivered by God himself to Moses, and by Moses made known to the people. Before that time there was no written law of God, who, as yet having not chosen any people to be his peculiar kingdom, had given no law to men but the law of nature — that is, the precepts of natural reason, written in every man's own heart. Of these two tables, the first contains the law of sovereignty: (1) That they should not obey, nor honour, the gods of other nations, in these words: 'Non habebis Deos alienos coram me' — that is, 'You shall not have for gods, the gods that other nations worship; but only me' — whereby they were forbidden to obey, or to honour, as their king and governor, any other god than the one who spoke to them then by Moses, and afterwards by the high priest. (2) That 'they should not make any image to represent him' — that is, they were not to choose for themselves, neither in heaven nor on earth, any representative of their own fancying, but to obey Moses and Aaron, whom he had appointed to that office. (3) That 'they should not take the name of God in vain' — that is, they should not speak rashly of their king, nor dispute his right, nor the commissions of Moses and Aaron, his lieutenants. (4) That 'they should every seventh day abstain from their ordinary labour,' and employ that time in doing him public honour. The second table contains the duty of one man to another: 'To honour parents; not to kill; not to commit adultery; not to steal; not to corrupt judgement by false witness'; and finally, 'not so much as to design in their heart the doing of any injury one to another.' The question now is, who it was that gave to these written tables the obligatory force of laws. There is no doubt but they were made laws by God himself. But because a law does not oblige, nor is law, to any but to those who acknowledge it to be the act of the sovereign, how could the people of Israel — who were forbidden to approach the mountain to hear what God said to Moses — be obliged to obedience to all those laws which Moses propounded to them? Some of them were indeed the laws of nature, as all the second table, and therefore to be acknowledged for God's laws, not to the Israelites alone but to all peoples. But of those that were peculiar to the Israelites, as those of the first table, the question remains — save that they had obliged themselves, presently after the propounding of them, to obey Moses, in these words (Exod. 20:19): 'Speak you to us, and we will hear you; but let not God speak to us, lest we die.' It was therefore only Moses then, and after him the high priest, whom (by Moses) God declared should administer this his peculiar kingdom, who had on earth the power to make this short Scripture of the Decalogue to be law in the commonwealth of Israel. But Moses, and Aaron, and the succeeding high priests, were the civil sovereigns. So up to this point, the canonising — or making of the Scripture law — belonged to the civil sovereign.

The judicial law — that is, the laws God prescribed to the magistrates of Israel for the rule of their administration of justice, and of the sentences, or judgements, they should pronounce in pleas between man and man — and the Levitical law — that is, the rule God prescribed touching the rites and ceremonies of the priests and Levites — were all delivered to them by Moses only; and therefore also became laws by virtue of the same promise of obedience to Moses. Whether these laws were then written, or not written, but dictated to the people by Moses (after his forty days being with God in the mount) by word of mouth, is not expressed in the text. But they were all positive laws, and equivalent to Holy Scripture, and made canonical by Moses the civil sovereign.

After the Israelites had come into the plains of Moab over against Jericho, and were ready to enter into the land of promise, Moses added to the former laws several others, which are therefore called Deuteronomy — that is, second laws. And they are (as it is written, Deut. 29:1) 'The words of a covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel, besides the covenant which he made with them in Horeb.' For, having explained those former laws in the beginning of the book of Deuteronomy, he adds others, that begin at chapter 12 and continue to the end of chapter 26 of the same book. This law (Deut. 27:1) they were commanded to write on great stones plastered over, at their passing over the Jordan. This law also was written by Moses himself in a book, and delivered into the hands of the 'priests, and to the elders of Israel' (Deut. 31:9), and commanded (verse 26) 'to be put in the side of the ark'; for in the ark itself was nothing but the Ten Commandments. This was the law which Moses (Deut. 17:18) commanded the kings of Israel should keep a copy of; and this is the law which, having been long lost, was found again in the temple in the time of Josiah, and by his authority received as the law of God. But both Moses, at the writing, and Josiah, at the recovery of it, had the civil sovereignty. Up to this point, therefore, the power of making Scripture canonical was in the civil sovereign.

Besides this book of the law, there was no other book, from the time of Moses till after the captivity, received among the Jews for the law of God. For the prophets (except a few) lived in the time of the captivity itself; and the rest lived but a little before it; and were so far from having their prophecies generally received for laws, that their persons were persecuted, partly by false prophets, and partly by the kings who were seduced by them. And this book itself, which was confirmed by Josiah as the law of God, and with it all the history of the works of God, was lost in the captivity, and the sack of the city of Jerusalem, as appears by 2 Esdras 14:21: 'Your law is burnt; therefore no man knows the things that are done of you, or the works that shall begin.' And before the captivity, between the time when the law was lost (which is not mentioned in Scripture, but may probably be thought to be the time of Rehoboam, when Shishak king of Egypt took the spoils of the temple, 1 Kings 14:26) and the time of Josiah, when it was found again, they had no written word of God, but ruled according to their own discretion, or by the direction of such as each of them esteemed prophets.

From which we may infer that the Scriptures of the Old Testament which we have at this day were not canonical, nor a law to the Jews, until the renovation of their covenant with God at their return from the captivity, and the restoration of their commonwealth under Ezra. But from that time forward they were accounted the law of the Jews, and as such translated into Greek by seventy elders of Judea, and put into the library of Ptolemy at Alexandria, and approved as the word of God. Now since Ezra was the high priest, and the high priest was their civil sovereign, it is plain that the Scriptures were never made laws except by the sovereign civil power.

The New Testament began to be canonical under Christian sovereigns. By the writings of the fathers who lived in the time before Christian religion was received and authorised by the emperor Constantine, we may find that the books we now have of the New Testament were held by the Christians of that time (except a few, in respect of whose paucity the rest were called the Catholic Church, and others heretics) as the dictates of the Holy Ghost, and consequently as the canon, or rule, of faith. Such was the reverence and opinion they had of their teachers; as generally the reverence that disciples bear to their first masters, in every kind of doctrine they receive from them, is not small. There is therefore no doubt that when St Paul wrote to the churches he had converted, or any other apostle, or disciple of Christ, to those who had then embraced Christ, they received those writings of theirs for the true Christian doctrine. But in that time, when not the power and authority of the teacher, but the faith of the hearer, caused them to receive it, it was not the apostles who made their own writings canonical: every convert made them so to himself.

But the question here is not what any Christian made a law, or canon, to himself (which he might again reject by the same right by which he received it), but what was so made a canon to them that without injustice they could not do anything contrary to it. That the New Testament should in this sense be canonical — that is, a law in any place where the law of the commonwealth had not made it so — is contrary to the nature of a law. For a law (as has already been shown) is the commandment of the man, or assembly, to whom we have given sovereign authority, to make such rules for the direction of our actions as he shall think fit, and to punish us when we do anything contrary to them. When therefore any other man shall offer us any other rules which the sovereign ruler has not prescribed, they are but counsel and advice, which, whether good or bad, he that is counselled may, without injustice, refuse to observe; and when contrary to the laws already established, cannot, without injustice, observe them, however good he conceives them to be. I say he cannot in this case observe the same in his actions, nor in his discourse with other men, though he may without blame believe his private teachers, and wish he had the liberty to practise their advice, and that it were publicly received for law. For internal faith is in its own nature invisible, and consequently exempted from all human jurisdiction; whereas the words and actions that proceed from it, as breaches of our civil obedience, are injustice both before God and man. Seeing then our Saviour has denied his kingdom to be in this world, and has said he came not to judge, but to save, the world, he has not subjected us to other laws than those of the commonwealth — that is, the Jews to the law of Moses (which, he says, Matt. 5, he came not to destroy, but to fulfil), and other nations to the laws of their various sovereigns, and all men to the laws of nature; the observing of which, both he himself and his apostles in their teaching have recommended to us as a necessary condition of being admitted by him in the last day into his eternal kingdom, where there shall be protection, and life everlasting. Since then our Saviour and his apostles left not new laws to oblige us in this world, but new doctrine to prepare us for the next, the books of the New Testament, which contain that doctrine, until obedience to them was commanded by those whom God has given power to on earth to be legislators, were not obligatory canons — that is, laws — but only good and safe advice, for the direction of sinners in the way to salvation, which every man might take, and refuse, at his own peril, without injustice.

Again, our Saviour Christ's commission to his apostles and disciples was to proclaim his kingdom (not present, but) to come; and to teach all nations; and to baptise those who should believe; and to enter into the houses of those who should receive them; and where they were not received, to shake off the dust of their feet against them — but not to call for fire from heaven to destroy them, nor to compel them to obedience by the sword. In all of which there is nothing of power, but of persuasion. He sent them out as sheep among wolves, not as kings to their subjects. They had not in commission to make laws, but to obey, and teach obedience to, laws already made; and consequently they could not make their writings obligatory canons, without the help of the sovereign civil power. And therefore the Scripture of the New Testament is law only there, where the lawful civil power has made it so. And there also the king, or sovereign, makes it a law to himself; by which he subjects himself, not to the doctor, or apostle, who converted him, but to God himself, and his Son Jesus Christ, as immediately as did the apostles themselves.

What may seem to give the New Testament, in respect of those who have embraced Christian doctrine, the force of laws in the times and places of persecution, is the decrees they made among themselves in their synods. For we read (Acts 15:28) the style of the council of the apostles, the elders, and the whole church in this way: 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things, etc.' — which is a style that signifies a power to lay a burden on those who had received their doctrine. Now 'to lay a burden on another' seems the same as 'to oblige'; and so the acts of that council were laws to the then-Christians. Nevertheless they were no more laws than these other precepts: 'Repent; be baptised; keep the commandments; believe the gospel; come to me; sell all that you have; give it to the poor; and follow me,' which are not commands but invitations and callings of men to Christianity — like that of Isaiah 55:1, 'Ho, every one that thirsts, come to the waters; come, and buy wine and milk without money.' For, first, the apostles' power was no other than that of our Saviour: to invite men to embrace the kingdom of God, which they themselves acknowledged as a kingdom (not present, but) to come; and they that have no kingdom can make no laws. And secondly, if their acts of council were laws, they could not without sin be disobeyed. But we read nowhere that those who did not receive the doctrine of Christ thereby sinned, but that they died in their sins — that is, that their sins against the laws to which they owed obedience were not pardoned. And those laws were the laws of nature, and the civil laws of the state, to which every Christian man had by pact submitted himself. And so by the burden which the apostles might lay on those they had converted are not to be understood laws, but conditions, proposed to those who sought salvation; which they might accept or refuse at their own peril, without a new sin, though not without the hazard of being condemned and excluded from the kingdom of God for their past sins. And so of infidels St John says, not that the wrath of God shall 'come' upon them, but 'the wrath of God remains upon them'; and not that they shall be condemned, but that 'they are condemned already' (John 3:36, 3:18). Nor can it be conceived that the benefit of faith 'is remission of sins' unless we conceive withal that the damage of infidelity 'is the retention of the same sins.'

But to what end is it (some may ask) that the apostles, and other pastors of the church after their time, should meet together to agree on what doctrine should be taught — both for faith and for manners — if no man were obliged to observe their decrees? To this it may be answered that the apostles, and elders of that council, were obliged, even by their entrance into it, to teach the doctrine concluded and decreed in it to be taught, so far as no precedent law to which they were obliged to yield obedience was to the contrary; but not that all other Christians should be obliged to observe what they taught. For though they might deliberate what each of them should teach, they could not deliberate what others should do, unless their assembly had had a legislative power, which none could have but civil sovereigns. For though God is the sovereign of all the world, we are not bound to take for his law whatever is propounded by every man in his name; nor anything contrary to the civil law, which God has expressly commanded us to obey.

Seeing then that the acts of council of the apostles were then no laws but counsels, much less are the acts of any other doctors, or councils, since (if assembled without the authority of the civil sovereign) laws. And consequently the books of the New Testament, though most perfect rules of Christian doctrine, could not be made laws by any other authority than that of kings, or sovereign assemblies.

The first council that made the Scriptures we now have canon is not extant; for that the collection of the first bishop of Rome after St Peter is subject to question. For though the canonical books are there reckoned up, the words 'Sint vobis omnibus Clericis et Laicis Libris venerandi, etc.' contain a distinction of clergy and laity that was not in use so near St Peter's time. The first council for settling the canonical Scripture that is extant is that of Laodicea, canon 59, which forbids the reading of other books than these in the churches — which is a mandate not addressed to every Christian, but only to those who had authority to read any books publicly in the church; that is, to ecclesiastics only.

Of ecclesiastical officers in the time of the apostles, some were magisterial, some ministerial. Magisterial were the offices of preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God to infidels; of administering the sacraments and divine service; and of teaching the rules of faith and manners to those who were converted. Ministerial was the office of deacons — that is, of those who were appointed to the administration of the secular necessities of the church, at such time as they lived on a common stock of money raised from the voluntary contributions of the faithful.

Among the officers magisterial, the first and principal were the apostles, of whom there were at first only twelve; and these were chosen and constituted by our Saviour himself. Their office was not only to preach, teach, and baptise, but also to be martyrs — that is, witnesses of our Saviour's resurrection. This testimony was the specific and essential mark by which the apostleship was distinguished from other ecclesiastical magistracy: as being necessary for an apostle either to have seen our Saviour after his resurrection, or to have conversed with him before, and seen his works, and other arguments of his divinity, by which they might be taken for sufficient witnesses. So at the election of a new apostle in the place of Judas Iscariot, St Peter says (Acts 1:21–22): 'Of these men who have accompanied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John to that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection' — where by the word 'must' is implied a necessary property of an apostle: to have accompanied with the first and prime apostles in the time when our Saviour manifested himself in the flesh.
Matthias made apostle by the congregation.

The first apostle of those not constituted by Christ while he was on earth was Matthias, chosen in this way. There were assembled together in Jerusalem about 120 Christians (Acts 1:15). These appointed two — Joseph the Just, and Matthias (verse 23) — and caused lots to be drawn; 'and (verse 26) the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the apostles.' So that here we see that the ordination of this apostle was the act of the congregation, and not of St Peter, nor of the eleven, otherwise than as members of the assembly.

After him there was never any other apostle ordained, except Paul and Barnabas, which was done (as we read Acts 13:1–3) in this way: 'There were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers — Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen (which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch), and Saul. As they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them." And when they had fasted, and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.'

By which it is plain that, though they were called by the Holy Ghost, their calling was declared to them, and their mission authorised, by the particular church of Antioch. And that this their calling was to the apostleship is plain from this, that they are both called (Acts 14:14) apostles. And that it was by virtue of this act of the church of Antioch that they were apostles, St Paul declares plainly (Rom. 1:1) in that he uses the word that the Holy Ghost used at his calling. For he styles himself 'an apostle separated unto the gospel of God' — alluding to the words of the Holy Ghost, 'Separate me Barnabas and Saul, etc.' But since the work of an apostle was to be a witness of the resurrection of Christ, a man may here ask how St Paul, who did not converse with our Saviour before his passion, could know he was risen. To this it is easily answered, that our Saviour himself appeared to him on the way to Damascus, from heaven, after his ascension, 'and chose him for a vessel to bear his name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel'; and consequently (having seen the Lord after his passion) he was a competent witness of his resurrection. And as for Barnabas, he was a disciple before the passion. It is therefore plain that Paul and Barnabas were apostles, and yet chosen and authorised (not by the first apostles alone, but) by the church of Antioch — as Matthias was chosen and authorised by the church of Jerusalem.

'Bishop,' a word formed in our language out of the Greek Episcopus, signifies an overseer, or superintendent, of any business — and particularly a pastor or shepherd. Thence by metaphor it was taken, not only among the Jews who were originally shepherds, but also among the heathen, to signify the office of a king, or any other ruler, or guide, of people, whether he ruled by laws or by doctrine. And so the apostles were the first Christian bishops, instituted by Christ himself; in which sense the apostleship of Judas is called (Acts 1:20) his bishopric. And afterwards, when there were constituted elders in the Christian churches, with charge to guide Christ's flock by their doctrine and advice, these elders were also called bishops. Timothy was an elder (which word 'elder' in the New Testament is a name of office, as well as of age); yet he was also a bishop. And bishops were then content with the title of elders. Nay, St John himself, the apostle beloved of our Lord, begins his second epistle with these words: 'The Elder to the Elect Lady.' By which it is plain that 'bishop,' 'pastor,' 'elder,' 'doctor' (that is to say, 'teacher'), were but so many different names of the same office in the time of the apostles. For there was then no government by coercion, but only by doctrine and persuasion. The kingdom of God was yet to come, in a new world; so that there could be no authority to compel in any church, until the commonwealth had embraced the Christian faith; and consequently no diversity of authority, though there was diversity of employments.

Besides these magisterial employments in the church — namely apostles, bishops, elders, pastors, and doctors, whose calling was to proclaim Christ to the Jews and the infidels, and to direct and teach those who believed — we read in the New Testament of no other. For by the names of 'evangelists' and 'prophets' is signified not any office, but various gifts, by which various men were profitable to the church. As evangelists, by writing the life and acts of our Saviour, such as were St Matthew and St John, apostles, and St Mark and St Luke, disciples (and whoever else wrote on that subject — as St Thomas, and St Barnabas, are said to have done, though the church has not received the books that have gone under their names). And as prophets, by the gift of interpreting the Old Testament, and sometimes by declaring their special revelations to the church. For neither these gifts, nor the gifts of tongues, nor the gift of casting out devils, or of curing other diseases, nor anything else made an officer in the church, save only the due calling and election to the charge of teaching.

As the apostles Matthias, Paul, and Barnabas were not made by our Saviour himself, but were elected by the church — that is, by the assembly of Christians (namely, Matthias by the church of Jerusalem, and Paul and Barnabas by the church of Antioch) — so also were the presbyters, and pastors in other cities, elected by the churches of those cities. For proof of which, let us consider, first, how St Paul proceeded in the ordination of presbyters in the cities where he had converted men to the Christian faith, immediately after he and Barnabas had received their apostleship. We read (Acts 14:23) that 'they ordained elders in every church'; which at first sight may be taken for an argument that they themselves chose, and gave them their authority. But if we consider the original text, it will be plain that they were authorised, and chosen, by the assembly of the Christians of each city. For the words there are cheirotonesantes autois presbyterous kat ekklesian — that is, 'When they had ordained them elders by the holding up of hands in every congregation.' Now it is well enough known that in all those cities, the manner of choosing magistrates and officers was by plurality of suffrages; and (because the ordinary way of distinguishing the affirmative votes from the negatives was by holding up of hands) to ordain an officer in any of the cities was no more than to bring the people together to elect them by plurality of votes — whether it were by plurality of elevated hands, or by plurality of voices, or by plurality of balls, beans, or small stones, of which every man cast one into a vessel marked for the affirmative, or negative; for various cities had various customs in that point. It was therefore the assembly that elected its own elders; the apostles were only presidents of the assembly, to call them together for such election, and to pronounce them elected, and to give them the benediction, which is now called consecration. And for this cause, those who were presidents of the assemblies — as (in the absence of the apostles) the elders were — were called proestotes, and in Latin antistites, which words signify the principal person of the assembly, whose office was to number the votes, and to declare thereby who was chosen; and where the votes were equal, to decide the matter in question by adding his own (which is the office of a president in council). And (because all the churches had their presbyters ordained in the same way), where the word is 'constitute' (as Titus 1:5), hina katasteses kata polin presbuterous, 'For this cause I left you in Crete, that you should constitute elders in every city,' we are to understand the same thing — namely, that he should call the faithful together, and ordain them presbyters by plurality of suffrages. It would have been a strange thing if in a town, where men perhaps had never seen any magistrate otherwise chosen than by an assembly, those of the town becoming Christians should so much as have thought of any other way of election of their teachers and guides — that is, of their presbyters (otherwise called bishops) — than this of plurality of suffrages, intimated by St Paul (Acts 14:23) in the word cheirotonesantes. Nor was there ever any choosing of bishops (before the emperors found it necessary to regulate them in order to the keeping of the peace among them), except by the assemblies of the Christians in every several town.

The same is also confirmed by the continual practice, even to this day, in the election of the bishops of Rome. For if the bishop of any place had the right of choosing another to the succession of the pastoral office in any city — at such time as he went from there to plant the same in another place — much more would he have had the right to appoint his successor in that place where he last resided and died. And we do not find that ever any bishop of Rome appointed his successor. For they were for a long time chosen by the people, as we may see by the sedition raised about the election between Damasus and Ursinicus; which Ammianus Marcellinus says was so great that Juventius the prefect, unable to keep the peace between them, was forced to go out of the city; and that there were above a hundred men found dead upon that occasion in the church itself. And though they were afterwards chosen, first by the whole clergy of Rome, and afterwards by the cardinals, yet never any was appointed to the succession by his predecessor. If therefore they claimed no right to appoint their successors, I think I may reasonably conclude they had no right to appoint the new power — which none could take from the church to bestow on them, but such as had a lawful authority not only to teach, but to command, the church; which none could do but the civil sovereign.

The word 'minister' in the original, diakonos, signifies one who voluntarily does the business of another man; and differs from a servant only in this, that servants are obliged by their condition to what is commanded them, whereas ministers are obliged only by their undertaking, and bound therefore to no more than that which they have undertaken. So that both those who teach the word of God, and those who administer the secular affairs of the church, are both ministers, but they are ministers of different persons. For the pastors of the church, called (Acts 6:4) 'the ministers of the word,' are ministers of Christ, whose word it is; but the ministry of a deacon, which is called (verse 2 of the same chapter) 'serving of tables,' is a service done to the church, or congregation. So neither any one man, nor the whole church, could ever say of their pastor that he was their minister; but of a deacon — whether the charge he undertook were to serve tables, or to distribute maintenance to the Christians when they lived in each city on a common stock, or on collections, as in the first times; or to take care of the house of prayer, or of the revenue, or other worldly business of the church — the whole congregation might properly call him their minister.

For their employment, as deacons, was to serve the congregation; though on occasion they did not refrain from preaching the gospel and maintaining the doctrine of Christ, every one according to his gifts, as St Stephen did, and both preaching and baptising as Philip did. For the Philip who (Acts 8:5) preached the gospel at Samaria, and (verse 38) baptised the eunuch, was Philip the deacon, not Philip the apostle. For it is plain (verse 1) that when Philip preached in Samaria, the apostles were at Jerusalem; and (verse 14) 'When they heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them' — by the imposition of whose hands those who were baptised (verse 15) received (what before, by the baptism of Philip, they had not received) the Holy Ghost. For it was necessary for the conferring of the Holy Ghost that their baptism should be administered, or confirmed, by a minister of the word, not by a minister of the church. And therefore, to confirm the baptism of those that Philip the deacon had baptised, the apostles sent out of their own number from Jerusalem to Samaria Peter and John, who conferred on those who had before been only baptised those graces that were signs of the Holy Spirit — which at that time accompanied all true believers. What these were may be understood from what St Mark says (chapter 16:17): 'These signs follow those that believe in my name: they shall cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents, and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover.' This Philip could not give; but the apostles could, and (as appears by this passage) effectually did, to every man who truly believed and was by a minister of Christ himself baptised — which power either Christ's ministers in this age cannot confer, or else there are very few true believers, or Christ has very few ministers.

That the first deacons were chosen, not by the apostles, but by a congregation of the disciples — that is, of Christian men of all sorts — is plain from Acts 6, where we read that the twelve, after the number of disciples had multiplied, called them together; and having told them it was not fit that the apostles should leave the word of God and serve tables, said to them (verse 3), 'Brethren, look you out among yourselves seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.' Here it is plain that, though the apostles declared them elected, the congregation chose them; which also (verse 5) is more expressly said, where it is written that 'the saying pleased the multitude, and they chose seven, etc.'

Under the Old Testament, the tribe of Levi alone was capable of the priesthood, and the other inferior offices of the church. The land was divided among the other tribes (Levi excepted), which by the subdivision of the tribe of Joseph into Ephraim and Manasseh were still twelve. To the tribe of Levi were assigned certain cities for their habitation, with the suburbs for their cattle; but for their portion, they were to have the tenth of the fruits of the land of their brethren. Again, the priests for their maintenance had the tenth of that tenth, together with part of the oblations and sacrifices. For God had said to Aaron (Numb. 18:20): 'You shall have no inheritance in their land, nor shall you have any part among them; I am your part, and your inheritance among the children of Israel.' For God being then king, and having constituted the tribe of Levi to be his public ministers, he allowed them for their maintenance the public revenue — that is, the part God had reserved to himself, which were tithes and offerings; and that is what is meant where God says, 'I am your inheritance.' And therefore to the Levites might not unfitly be attributed the name of clergy, from kleros, which signifies lot, or inheritance — not that they were heirs of the kingdom of God more than any other, but that God's inheritance was their maintenance. Now seeing that in this time God himself was their king, and Moses, Aaron, and the succeeding high priests were his lieutenants, it is plain that the right of tithes and offerings was constituted by the civil power.

After their rejection of God in the demand of a king, they still enjoyed the same revenue; but the right of it was derived from this, that the kings never took it from them. For the public revenue was at the disposing of him who was the public person; and that (till the captivity) was the king. And again, after the return from the captivity, they paid their tithes as before to the priest. So up to this point, church livings were determined by the civil sovereign.
